Keyed digest and constant-time comparison (C backend)

Source: R/digest_extra.R
keyeddgst.Rd

chmac() computes HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 2104), a digest of a message under a secret key, and cdgsteq() compares two digests without leaking through timing how much of them matched. Use the pair to sign a manifest or a capsule with a shared secret and to check a signature someone hands you.

Usage

chmac(key, msg)

cdgsteq(a, b)

Arguments

key

Secret key, as a length-1 character vector or a raw vector. Keys longer than the 64-byte block are hashed down first, per RFC 2104. Use at least 32 bytes of real entropy; against a quantum adversary Grover halves the effective key strength, so a 256-bit key retains a 128-bit margin.

msg

Message to authenticate, as a length-1 character vector (its bytes) or a raw vector.

a, b

Digests to compare, each a length-1 character vector.

Value

chmac() a length-1 character vector: 64 lowercase hex characters. cdgsteq() a length-1 logical; FALSE when the two differ in length.

Details

The difference from a plain csha256() is AUTHENTICATION – anyone can recompute a SHA-256 and so anyone can forge one after editing a manifest, but only a holder of the key can produce a matching HMAC. This is what makes cpssign()'s "hmac" scheme meaningful. The construction is $$\mathrm{HMAC}(K, m) = H((K' \oplus opad) \| H((K' \oplus ipad) \| m))$$ with \(H\) = SHA-256, \(K'\) the key padded to the 64-byte block (or hashed first when longer), \(ipad\) = 0x36 and \(opad\) = 0x5c repeated. The results match the RFC 4231 test vectors.

cdgsteq() compares two digests in constant time (verified under valgrind memcheck in CI with both inputs marked secret: inst/ctcheck, case digest-equal). Use it instead of == whenever the comparison is against a value an attacker supplied: a short-circuiting comparison leaks, through its own timing, how many leading characters were correct, which is enough to recover a tag byte by byte. It compares the strings exactly, so case matters ("ABC" is not "abc"): lower-case both first if the digests may come in either case.

Errors: key or msg that is neither one non-NA string nor a raw vector; a or b that is not one non-NA string.

References

Krawczyk H, Bellare M, Canetti R (1997). HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication. RFC 2104. doi:10.17487/RFC2104

Examples

# RFC 4231 test case 2.
chmac("Jefe", "what do ya want for nothing?")
#> [1] "5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843"

# The key changes the digest, so a manifest cannot be re-signed
# without it.
chmac("key-a", "manifest")
#> [1] "463b8b2c47caadd6334c53e4d9492fdac6fcaca185f56229043e1a025138ceae"
chmac("key-b", "manifest")
#> [1] "f3ebaf1b8fad504c57fd4cf82b163e30eac6eabd31b7c41a2a6e268ec445b134"

# Raw keys and messages are accepted.
chmac(as.raw(rep(0x0b, 20)), "Hi There")
#> [1] "b0344c61d8db38535ca8afceaf0bf12b881dc200c9833da726e9376c2e32cff7"

# Compare tags in constant time, never with ==.
tag <- chmac("k", "m")
cdgsteq(tag, chmac("k", "m"))
#> [1] TRUE
cdgsteq(tag, chmac("k", "tampered"))
#> [1] FALSE
cdgsteq(tag, "too-short")
#> [1] FALSE

# one message at a time
try(chmac("k", c("m1", "m2")))
#> Error : chmac: `msg` must be a length-1 character vector or a raw vector
